title: Greed and generosity

segments.voice: Yesterday, acedia, the noonday demon: the monks' heavy boredom with good things. Your line was the noonday demon.

Every morning in the wilderness, bread is lying on the ground. The Israelites call it manna. The instruction is simple: gather what you need for today, and keep none till morning. Some of them keep some anyway. Just in case. And the next morning, "it bred worms, and stank." The bread that fed them, stored up, went bad overnight. And the ones who gathered a lot? The text says they had nothing left over. The ones who gathered a little had enough.

Greed is a closed hand. It gathers, and then it grips. Often it's less about wanting more things than about fear: what if there isn't enough tomorrow? The manna story answers that fear strangely. The hoard doesn't protect you; the daily gathering does. Jesus says it plainly in Luke: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." Your life isn't the pile. For the opposite, the Bible uses hands. In Deuteronomy, the law turns to the poor among the people: don't "shut thine hand from thy poor brother," but "thou shalt open thine hand wide." Not a little. Wide. Much later, Paul goes back to the manna. He's collecting money for a poor church in Jerusalem, and he quotes the old story: "He that had gathered much had nothing over; and he that had gathered little had no lack." For Paul, the manna pictures sharing: what one has too much of, another needs, and generosity evens it out. He adds one more thing: "God loveth a cheerful giver." Not dutiful, not guilty. Gladly, without counting first. So generosity is less about the size of a gift than the shape of the hand. A closed hand can hold on to a lot, but it can't receive anything either. An open hand can let go, and it's ready to be filled. Christians practice this through tithes, offerings, alms, or quiet gifts nobody sees. The shape is the same.

Picture your shelves, your closet, your calendar, and let one thing come to mind you could give that you hadn't planned to: some money, a coat you don't wear, an hour, a meal for someone. Don't weigh it too long. If you pray, you can offer it with Paul's phrase: a cheerful giver.
Greed and generosity. The closed hand that hoards out of fear, and the open hand that lets go and can be filled.
Your line: open hands. Like the manna, enough for today really can be enough. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Isn't greed just being rich? I'm not rich, so I'm fine, right?
options: It's less about the pile than the grip. Greed is a closed hand, often holding on from fear.
Right. Greed is about how much you own, so it's only a worry for wealthy people.
Kind of. Greed only means stealing; if you earned it, keeping it all can't be greed.
chat.meaning: Greed is a closed hand that grips, often out of fear. Like the hoarded manna, the pile doesn't protect you; an open hand can be filled.
